summary: This standards-track RFC defines the Router Information Link State Advertisement for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3, which lets routers advertise optional capabilities to others in the routing domain. Knowing what neighbors and other routers support helps with features that not everyone has.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers often need to know whether the other routers around them support a particular optional feature, such as traffic engineering or a graceful restart. This RFC gives OSPF a way to say so, in one advertisement in which a router lists the features it supports, and it separates the features that are only informative from the ones that change how the protocol runs.

questions: what is the ospf router information lsa
what is the ospf router functional capabilities tlv
subtitle: One OSPF advertisement in which a router lists the optional features it supports.

tldr.problem: Routers in an OSPF domain often need to know what optional features their neighbours support, but in OSPFv2 every bit of the options field in the advertisements has already been allocated.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the Router Information LSA, a new advertisement that carries capability bits in type, length, value records. In OSPFv2 it is an Opaque LSA of type 4, and in OSPFv3 it is an LSA with function code 12.
tldr.outcome: The RFC replaces RFC 4970, adding support for more than one instance of the advertisement and a second record for capabilities that change how the protocol behaves.

facts.label: TLV alignment
facts.value: 4 octets, padding not counted in the length

today: RFC 7770 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It replaced RFC 4970, whose definition of the same advertisement it keeps in most respects.

sections.title: Why Routers Should Advertise Their Capabilities
sections.content:
It is useful for routers in an OSPFv2 or OSPFv3 routing domain to know the capabilities of their neighbours and of other routers in the same domain, for both advertising and discovering OSPF capabilities.

OSPF already has a place for this: the options field in link state advertisements and in Hello packets carries optional router capabilities. In OSPFv2, however, every bit in that field has been allocated, so no further optional capability can be advertised there. This document therefore extends OSPF to advertise optional capabilities through Opaque LSAs in OSPFv2 and through LSAs with a unique type in OSPFv3.

For the capabilities OSPF already has, backwards compatibility rules mean this new advertisement is used mainly for information. For future OSPF extensions, the RFC says it may be used as the only way to advertise and discover a capability.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF has a small set of flags in its advertisements that say what a router can do, but in OSPFv2 every one of those flags is already taken. This RFC adds a separate advertisement so that new features can announce themselves without changing the old one.

sections.title: The Router Information LSA
sections.content:
In OSPFv2, a router advertises a link-scoped, area-scoped or AS-scoped Opaque LSA. The RI LSA has an Opaque type of 4, and the Opaque ID carries the RI LSA instance ID, with the first instance always having an instance ID of 0. The Opaque LSA type in the header is 9, 10 or 11 depending on the scope: link, area or AS.

In OSPFv3, the RI LSA has a function code of 12, and the S1 and S2 bits in the LSA type depend on the flooding scope wanted. The U bit is set, meaning the LSA is flooded even if the receiver does not understand it. The link state ID holds the instance ID.

In both versions, the first instance, instance 0, should always carry the Router Informational Capabilities TLV and, when it is advertised, the Router Functional Capabilities TLV. Later instances carry information that does not fit in the first one. OSPFv3 routers may advertise several RI LSAs per flooding scope.

The body of the advertisement holds one or more nested type, length, value records, the same format used by the traffic engineering extensions to OSPF.
sections.plainLanguage: The new advertisement comes in two shapes, one for each version of OSPF, but it carries the same kind of information in both. It carries a list of records, and the first advertisement of the list is the one that holds the standard set of capabilities.

sections.title: The TLV Format
sections.content:
The body of an RI LSA consists of one or more nested type, length, value records. Each record has a 16-bit Type field, a 16-bit Length field and a value. The Length field gives the length of the value in octets, so a record with no value has a length of 0. The record is padded to four-octet alignment, and the padding is not counted in the Length field: a three-octet value has a length of 3 but a total size of eight octets. Nested records are aligned the same way, and the padding octets carry undefined bits. A receiver ignores record types it does not recognise.

The RFC also sets a rule for future work: any new RI LSA record must state in its own specification whether it applies to OSPFv2 only, OSPFv3 only, or to both.
sections.plainLanguage: Each capability is written in a small record that says what kind of capability it is, how long its value is, and then the value itself. Records are padded so that the next one starts on a neat boundary, and a router quietly skips any record type it does not know.

sections.title: Informational Capabilities
sections.content:
A router that advertises an RI LSA may include the Router Informational Capabilities TLV. If it does, it must be the first record in the first instance of the advertisement. The record must accurately reflect the router's capabilities in the scope advertised. These capabilities have no effect on how OSPF runs; they are purely for information.

The record's Type field is set to 1. Its Length field gives the length of the value in octets and is a multiple of four, initially 4, meaning four octets of capability bits. The value is a sequence of capability bits rounded up to a multiple of four octets and padded with undefined bits. The bits are numbered from left to right, with the most significant bit being bit 0.

The RFC assigns six bits: bit 0 is OSPF graceful restart capable, bit 1 is OSPF graceful restart helper, bit 2 is OSPF Stub Router support, bit 3 is OSPF Traffic Engineering support, bit 4 is OSPF point-to-point over LAN, and bit 5 is OSPF Experimental TE. Bits 6 to 31 are unassigned and are reserved for future assignment through IETF Review. The record may be followed by optional records that give more detail about a capability.
sections.plainLanguage: This record is a checklist of extra features the router supports, such as being able to restart without dropping traffic or taking part in traffic engineering. The list is only informative, so other routers read it but do not change their behaviour because of it.

sections.title: Functional Capabilities
sections.content:
The RFC also defines a Router Functional Capabilities TLV. A router advertising an RI LSA may include it, and if it does, it must be in the first instance of the advertisement. Unlike the informational record, this one must reflect the router's actual functional capabilities, because the information will be used to dictate OSPF protocol operation in the flooding scope of the advertisement that carries it. If the record is absent, or its length does not include the assigned bit for a capability, that capability is implicitly advertised as not supported by the advertising router.

The format matches the informational record: the Type field is set to 2, the Length field is a multiple of four octets and initially 4, and the value is a sequence of capability bits padded with undefined bits and numbered from the most significant bit as bit 0. The record may be followed by optional records that further specify a capability.

The difference matters. The OSPF extensions advertised in the functional record may be used by other OSPF routers to dictate protocol operation, and the specifications for those capabilities must describe protocol behaviour and address backwards compatibility. The RFC leaves the functional capability bits empty for now: the registry for them starts empty and is available for future capabilities, with additions assigned through IETF Review.
sections.plainLanguage: Some features change the rules of the protocol itself, and those belong in a separate record. A router that does not include a feature in that record is treated as not supporting it, so other routers can rely on the list before they rely on the feature.

sections.title: Choosing a Flooding Scope
sections.content:
The flooding scope of an RI LSA is set by its type. In OSPFv2, a type 9 Opaque LSA is link-scoped, type 10 is area-scoped and type 11 is AS-scoped. In OSPFv3, the S1 and S2 bits in the LSA type determine the scope. If AS-wide flooding is chosen, the originating router should also advertise area-scoped LSAs into any attached Not-So-Stubby Area, and a router may advertise different capabilities in those area-scoped advertisements than in the AS-scoped one. That lets a capability be limited in scope: a router that is an area border router might support traffic engineering in only some of the areas it touches.

The scope is the advertising router's choice and is a matter of local policy. The originating router may advertise several RI LSAs with the same instance ID as long as their scopes differ. The rules about which scopes a given record may be flooded in will be set record by record, and each future record's specification has to state them.
sections.plainLanguage: Each advertisement says how far it should travel: to the routers on one link, to the routers in one area, or to every router in the network. A router chooses this itself, and it can send different capabilities to different parts of the network when a feature is only supported in some of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC describes both a general mechanism for advertising router capabilities and the two records used for informational and functional capabilities. The capability records are less critical than the topology information that the base OSPF protocol already advertises. The security considerations for the general mechanism depend on how it is used in future, and should therefore be described as further capabilities are proposed. The security considerations for OSPF itself are covered in the base specifications for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.

On backwards compatibility, previously advertised Router Information records should continue to be advertised in the first instance of the advertisement, instance 0. If a record is advertised in more than one instance, and the RFC that defines it does not say how multiple instances are handled, then the instance with the numerically smallest instance ID is used and the later instances are ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The capability list is less sensitive than the routing information itself, so the RFC leaves the detailed security analysis to the specifications that add new capabilities. It also keeps old advertisements working: a capability that was already advertised stays in the first advertisement, and if the same capability turns up in several, the first one by number wins.

sections.title: Registry Assignments
sections.content:
The RFC asks IANA to point the reference for the OSPFv2 Opaque LSA type registry entry at this document instead of RFC 4970, and to do the same for the registry of OSPFv3 LSA function codes and the registry of Router Information record types.

For OSPFv3 LSA function codes, values 1 to 11 and 13 to 15 have already been assigned, and value 12 is assigned to the OSPFv3 Router Information LSA. The RFC also sets out the assignment policy: value 0 is reserved and not to be assigned, values 16 to 255 are unassigned and are now assigned through IETF Review rather than by Standards Action, values 256 to 8175 are reserved with no assignments, values 8176 to 8183 are for experimentation and must not be mentioned in RFCs, values 8184 to 8190 are for vendor private use, and value 8191 is reserved. An LSA with a function code in the vendor private use range must carry the Enterprise Code as the first four octets after the 20 octets of the LSA header. A new function code's documentation must state the valid combinations of the U, S2 and S1 bits and should say how the link state ID is assigned.

For Router Information record types, values 3 to 9 have already been assigned, value 1 is the Router Informational Capabilities record and value 2 is the Router Functional Capabilities record. Value 0 is reserved, values 10 to 32767 are unassigned and are assigned through IETF Review, values 32768 to 32777 are for experimentation, and values 32778 to 65535 are reserved until a Standards Track RFC covers them. Two further registries hold the capability bits themselves: one for the informational capability bits and one, newly created as a subregistry of the OSPFv2 parameters, for the functional capability bits, which starts out empty.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC sorts out the numbering: which numbers are free for new capabilities, which are reserved, and which are for experiments or for vendors. It also decides that new entries are reviewed by the IETF rather than simply announced by the IANA.

items.title: Link scope
items.text: OSPFv2 type 9: the LSA stays on the link it was sent on.

items.title: Area scope
items.text: OSPFv2 type 10: the LSA reaches the routers of one area.

items.title: AS scope
items.text: OSPFv2 type 11: the LSA reaches every router in the autonomous system.

items.title: Same instance, different scopes
items.text: A router may advertise several RI LSAs with the same instance ID if their scopes differ.
